common_name: Krupnopladnaya Kolomikta Kiwi (Large-Fruited Russian Arctic Beauty Kiwi)

planting.note: Plant a rooted cutting or grafted vine of Krupnopladnaya in spring against a sturdy trellis in humus-rich, well-drained, non-alkaline soil, and site a male kolomikta vine within range since this is a fruiting female selection that will not set fruit alone.

directions: Krupnopladnaya (Russian for 'large-fruited') is a Russian selection of Actinidia kolomikta chosen specifically for fruit size well above the species average, while retaining the vine's exceptional cold hardiness. Grow it on a trellis, arbor, or fence in fertile, well-drained soil with dappled light, since strong afternoon sun can scorch the foliage in warmer climates. The grape-sized, smooth green kiwiberries ripen unevenly over several weeks in late summer and drop when ripe, so harvest daily from a tarp or by hand-picking softened fruit. Because the species is dioecious, pair one male vine with several Krupnopladnaya females for reliable, heavy fruit set.
sources: Cornell University Cooperative Extension -- Kiwi Vine
University of Minnesota Extension -- Hardy Kiwi

common_name: Pineapple Crush Alpine Strawberry (White-Fruited Pineapple-Flavored Woodland Strawberry)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; surface-sow the fine seed and keep it consistently moist and in bright light until germination.

directions: Pineapple Crush is a white-fruited alpine strawberry whose creamy, blush-tinged berries carry a distinctive tropical pineapple aroma rather than the typical wild-strawberry flavor. Like other alpine types it forms tidy, runnerless mounds that fruit continuously from early summer through fall once established, making it a good edging or container plant as well as a producer. Because the pale fruit doesn't visually signal ripeness to birds the way red berries do, losses to birds are usually lighter than with red alpine strawberries, though the soft fruit still bruises easily and should be picked and eaten promptly. Transplant seedlings into humus-rich, well-drained soil with morning sun and afternoon shade in hot regions.

common_name: Reine des Vallees Alpine Strawberry (Classic French Everbearing Woodland Strawberry)

planting.note: Start seed indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost; the fine seed needs light and steady surface moisture to germinate evenly.

directions: Reine des Vallees ('Queen of the Valleys') is a 19th-century French heirloom alpine strawberry long prized for its intensely perfumed, slender conical red berries, considered by many growers among the most flavorful of the runnerless alpine types. Plants form neat, compact clumps well suited to edging borders, herb gardens, or containers, and bear continuously from early summer into fall without needing to manage runners. Set transplants in rich, well-drained soil with a bit of afternoon shade in hot climates, and pick berries often since the delicate fruit softens quickly once ripe. Division of established clumps every few years helps maintain vigor and fruit size.

common_name: Redstone Cornelian Cherry (Cold-Hardy Large-Fruited Cornus mas Selection)

planting.note: Plant a container-grown or bare-root grafted tree in early spring while still dormant; Redstone was selected for heavier, larger-fruited crops than seedling cornelian cherries and fruits more reliably with a second cultivar nearby for cross-pollination.

directions: Redstone is a fruit-improved selection of Cornus mas chosen for larger, deep-red, heavier-cropping fruit compared to unselected seedlings. Like the species, it opens small yellow flower clusters on bare branches in very early spring, well ahead of forsythia, then ripens its tart, plum-flavored fruit by midsummer, dropping as it softens so most growers gather it from a tarp shaken beneath the tree or by daily hand-picking. The fruit is prized for syrup, jam, sauces, and Eastern European-style preserves, and the tree itself tolerates poor soils, urban pollution, and drought once established with minimal pest or disease pressure. Plant it alongside another cornelian cherry cultivar for the fullest fruit set.

common_name: Flava Yellow Cornelian Cherry (Golden-Fruited Cornus mas Selection)

planting.note: Plant a container-grown or bare-root grafted tree in early spring while dormant; Flava is a long-recognized yellow-fruited form of Cornus mas grown for its milder, less astringent fruit and bright golden fall display of berries.

directions: Flava is the classic yellow-fruited form of cornelian cherry dogwood, producing translucent golden-amber fruit instead of the species' typical cherry red. The fruit is generally milder and less tart than red-fruited seedlings, making it more pleasant to eat fresh off the tree in addition to its use in preserves and syrups. Like other cornelian cherries it flowers on bare stems in late winter to earliest spring, tolerates a wide range of soils and urban conditions, and is largely trouble-free once established. Because its fruit color makes it stand out clearly against foliage, Flava also doubles as a distinctive landscape and hedgerow specimen alongside red-fruited cultivars.
sources: Dirr's Manual of Woody Landscape Plants
